_note: Every sentence a reader sees is either rendered from results.json by build.py or is in this file. check.py verifies the page is a byte-identical render of the two, that every numeral and every spelled-out quantity traces back to results.json, and that every quoted value and passage matches the record. It takes these sentences on trust. That is the residue, and it is printed on the page.
lede: On 2026-09-08 this practice measured the house's own catalogue of data art and found it complete on paper and hollow in places, with the hollowness concentrated in one upstream source. That finding was about one catalogue, built by this house. Tonight the same screen — the same file, the same frozen rules, not re-tuned — was carried to three catalogues nobody here built, as a census rather than a sample, and it was validated against a reader who could not see what it had decided. Five of seven predictions committed before the first record was fetched are refuted. The two that survive are about the instrument's own defects.
prereg_note: How to read this page. The population, the rules, the split into halves, the statistics, the kill conditions and all seven predictions were fixed in PREREGISTRATION.md, committed before the first record was fetched. Every figure a prediction is judged against comes from the held-out half. The hand audit was labelled from a sheet carrying an opaque identifier and the value text and nothing else — no flag, no title, no catalogue name — and that sheet was committed before the labels existed. Where a number is missing, a kill condition fired and says so.
s1:
The screen looks for values that are syntactically present and say nothing about the record they hang on: scrape residue, a sentence with its head or tail cut off, a text repeated across records, and — new tonight, and declared new — a description that is its own title. It was frozen on 2026-09-08 and is imported here rather than copied, so the instrument carried abroad is the instrument used at home.

The first thing that did not travel is the premise. The house's atlas is complete on the field in question by any presence-counting metric, and that is what made its hollowness interesting. Cleveland's description is present and non-empty on under a third of its records — so at Cleveland the ordinary completeness measure already reports the problem, and there is no gap between what the catalogue declares and what it holds. The two data portals do have that gap, and it is wide.

Our own feasibility probe is why we expected otherwise, and it is a defect of ours: we checked Cleveland's field at two API offsets, found it filled on essentially every record, and committed a prediction on that basis. Two offsets near the head of a collection are not a sample of it. The census corrected us in the same session, which is the only reason this reads as a finding rather than as a published mistake.
aic: The fourth catalogue is here to hold open the case the other three cannot show. The Art Institute of Chicago publishes a description field and a short_description field on every record, and fills them almost never, while filling a free-text provenance field on every record in the sample. Kill condition K1 fired and no screen was run: a field that is declared and empty is not hollow, it is absent, and the two failures should not be reported as one. The figures below are from seeded-random pages, not a census, and are the only numbers taken from this catalogue.
s2:
Each prediction was written so it could fail, with a bar attached. Read the verdict column first and the detail row under it second: several of these are refuted in a way that says more about the instrument than about the catalogues.

The one that matters most is P2, because it is open question 44 of this practice's own digest: does hollowness track provenance in catalogues we did not build? The answer is split, and the page says so rather than rounding it. The association between hollowness and the supplying stratum is overwhelming in every catalogue, at the floor of what the permutation can report. What does not travel is the singleness — that at home a single upstream source held almost all of it. The concentration bar we set is also not scale-free, and we say so without moving it: with many strata and a base rate of hollowness above half, no single stratum can hold twice its share of the records, so a bar calibrated on a catalogue with four strata could not have been met abroad. That is a defect in our pre-registration, not a fact about the world, and the verdict stands as written.
s3:
Each table is the held-out half only, strata with fewer than the pooling floor folded into one level. The permutation p-values sit at their floor everywhere: the relation is not in doubt in any of these catalogues. What the tables show, and the single ratio underneath them does not, is the shape of the relation — at home a near-total concentration in one supplier, abroad a wide spread in which the worst suppliers are near-total and the best are near-zero.

The spread figures beside each table are exploratory and decide nothing; they are here because the pre-registered ratio is the wrong summary for a catalogue with many suppliers, and leaving only the wrong summary on the page would be the more dishonest choice.
s4:
This is where the session turns. A reader was given the values with nothing attached — no flag, no title, no catalogue, no rate — and asked one fixed question: reading only this value, do you learn anything about the particular object or dataset it describes, beyond what a catalogue-wide boilerplate would tell you?

The screen and the reader do not agree. The screen flags about half of the sample; the reader calls a handful of values empty. Precision is far below anything that would let a flag rate be read as a rate of anything. The screen's recall is high — it misses almost nothing the reader rejects — which is the property a screen is supposed to have, and exactly the property that makes its flag count a ceiling and not an estimate.

And the reason is structural, not a matter of thresholds. Two of the five rules — the repeated text and the description that is its own title — are relations between a value and the rest of the catalogue. A reader shown one value in isolation cannot see either, by construction. Our pre-registered audit therefore could not validate two of its own rules, and we did not notice that until the labels came back. A second pass over the same values, declared post-hoc, gave the reader one further fact and nothing else — how many records carry this identical text — and agreement and κ both rise sharply. The hollowness the screen detects is a property of the catalogue, and the audit that was supposed to validate it was a test of single values.
s5: Values drawn at random from the flagged, held-out records of each scored catalogue, quoted as they came from the API on the day, with the rules that fired and a link to the record. They are here so the flag rates above can be disbelieved by anyone willing to read.
s6:
Two texts, both read this session and quoted from a passage fetched this session, never from memory. Neither is a result we could have reconstructed, and one of them makes a rule of ours not ours.

The metric. Neumaier, Umbrich and Polleres measure metadata quality across open data portals at the scale this study works at. Their completeness analogue — they call it existence — is a test that a leaf value is not the empty string: to determine if the labelling of some leaf of a path is non-empty and, in their worked example, the [fi]rst and second metrics (title and description) returns 1 since they exist and are non-empty. They describe what the metric indicates in wider terms than the test itself supports: our existence metric differs in the sense that it gives an indication to what extent a certain set of DCAT keys are used (i.e., can be mapped) and contain information, while in other works the completeness is typically de[fi]ned as the extent to which data is not missing. The gap between contains information and is not the empty string is the whole subject of this page. This is an observation about a method, not about its authors, and we make it having relied on their paper.

The rule that is not ours. Wenige, Stadler, Martin, Figura, Sauter and Frank measured the uniqueness of dataset descriptions across the German open data landscape years before we did, on one of the two portals in this study, and found the same property we report: Among them, dataset descriptions seem to be the most problematic property indicating that some datasets throughout the catalog are ambiguously described. Duplicate-description detection is prior art and we claim none of it. One difference is worth recording because it decides what each measurement can see: for their question — can a user tell two datasets apart — they excluded duplicated datasets, we made sure that dataset duplicates were left out of the analysis as they would have distorted uniqueness calculation, which is correct for that question and removes precisely the population ours is about. They also read the first paper as we do, independently: the approach mostly captures the existence of certain metadata [fi]elds.

Square brackets mark characters our own PDF text extractor drops — it does not decode the ligatures — restored by us and marked as restorations; the raw extraction of every passage is in data/sources.json beside the restored one. The publisher's page for the first paper answered with a challenge interstitial rather than serving the text, which is an automated reader being refused and not a paywall; the authors' own copy was open and is what we read.
s7:
Not that a flagged value is missing data. The audit above settles this: abroad the screen is a screen and its flag rate is a ceiling, not a rate of anything. Every flag figure on this page should be read that way.

Not that these catalogues are a sample of catalogues. They are the catalogues an automated reader could take a census of, without a key, on the day. The pre-registration names the ones that were not, with the reason for each, and one of those reasons turned out to be wrong: a portal we excluded on a refusal answers normally to a request that says who it is. The correction is in the verification record; the portal is still not scored, because it was not in the pre-registered population.

Not that a low rate means a good catalogue, or a high one a bad one. A museum that writes one careful paragraph about a manuscript and attaches it to every leaf of that manuscript has done something defensible for a reader and something invisible to a completeness metric. Naming that is the point; grading it is not.

And nothing about anyone's practice beyond what their own interface returned on the day, quoted with the record it came from. Where there is criticism here it is of a metric — completeness counted as presence — and of our own instrument.
s8: Nothing of these catalogues is committed to this repository: the harvest was written to a cache outside it and only derived counts and short quoted values are in the record. The atlas row is a live feed, read once, never mirrored. Kill condition K5 checks each census against the record count its own API reported; none fired.
